summary: Describes a backward-compatible technique for OSPF to exchange arbitrary data between neighbors on a link, called link-local signaling. OSPF packet formats were too rigid for new features, so this adds an extensible block.

plainLanguage.summary:
OSPF has a fixed set of packet types, each with a fixed layout, so there was nowhere to put information that a new feature wanted to exchange between two neighbouring routers.

This RFC adds a small optional block at the end of the two packets OSPF already sends while forming an adjacency. Inside the block are numbered triplets, each holding a type, a length and some data. A single bit in the packet header says the block is there, so a router that does not understand it simply ignores it.

questions: what is the ospf lls block
which ospf packets can carry lls data
subtitle: A way for routers on the same link to pass extra information to each other.

tldr.problem: OSPF packets have a fixed format, so there was no room for a new feature that needs to exchange arbitrary data between neighbouring routers. A new packet type would have meant more packets on the network and compatibility trouble.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an optional block of type, length and value triplets to the end of OSPF Hello and Database Description packets. A new bit in the Options field says the block is present, and a checksum covers it.
tldr.outcome: Neighbours can now exchange small amounts of extra information without changing the protocol or disturbing routers that do not understand it. The block may also be cryptographically authenticated with the same key as the rest of the OSPFv2 packet. The RFC obsoletes the experimental RFC 4813.

facts.value: A checksum and a length field, 16 bits each

today: RFC 5613 is a Proposed Standard from August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4813, bringing the experimental link-local signaling specification onto the Standards Track, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needed a Way to Carry Extra Data
sections.content:
OSPF is a link-state intra-domain routing protocol. Its routers exchange information on a link using packets that follow a well-defined fixed format. That format is not flexible enough to enable new features that need to exchange arbitrary data.

The document describes a backward-compatible technique to perform link-local signaling, that is, to exchange arbitrary data on a link. One potential way of solving the task could be introducing a new packet type, but that would mean introducing extra packets on the network that may not be desirable and may cause backward compatibility issues. The document therefore describes how to exchange data using standard OSPF packet types.

The extension applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. Throughout the document, OSPF is used when the text applies to both, and OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 when the text is protocol specific. The document does not specify how the data transmitted by the mechanism should be interpreted by OSPF routers, and it notes that routers that do not understand LLS may receive these packets, and that changes made because of the block's triplets do not affect basic routing when interacting with those routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule was that the routing protocol itself must not change. Any new feature has to fit inside the packets OSPF already sends, and a router that has never heard of the feature must carry on working.

sections.title: The LLS Data Block and the L-Bit
sections.content:
To perform link-local signaling, OSPF routers add a special data block to the end of OSPF packets, or right after the authentication data block when cryptographic authentication is used. The length of the LLS block is not included in the length of the OSPF packet, but it is included in the IPv4 or IPv6 packet length.

The block may be attached to OSPF Hello and Database Description packets. It must not be attached to any other OSPF packet types on generation, and must be ignored on reception.

The data included in a Hello packet may be used for dynamic signaling, since Hello packets may be sent at any time, but delivery of LLS data in Hello packets is not guaranteed. The data sent with Database Description packets is guaranteed to be delivered as part of the adjacency forming process.

A new L-bit, where L stands for LLS, is introduced into the OSPF Options field. Routers set it in Hello and Database Description packets to indicate that the packet contains an LLS data block, so the block is only examined if the bit is set. The bit must not be set except in Hello and Database Description packets that contain such a block.

The block itself begins with a checksum field holding the standard IP checksum for the entire contents of the block, computed after setting the checksum field to zero. If the checksum is incorrect, the OSPF packet must be processed, but the LLS block must be discarded. The 16-bit LLS Data Length field holds the length of the block, including header and payload, in 32-bit words. If the OSPF packet is cryptographically authenticated, the LLS block must also be cryptographically authenticated; in that case the regular checksum is not calculated and is set to zero instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The block rides along in the two packets used while an adjacency comes up. The Hello packet is cheap to send at any moment but its contents may be lost, while the database description packet is guaranteed to arrive during the handshake.

sections.title: The Type/Length/Value Triplets
sections.content:
The contents of an LLS data block are constructed using triplets, each with a Type field, a Length field and a Value field. The Type field contains the TLV identifier, which is unique for each type of TLV. The Length field contains the length of the Value field in bytes. The Value field is variable and contains arbitrary data.

All TLVs must be 32-bit aligned, with padding if necessary. TLVs are always padded to a 32-bit boundary, but the padding bytes are not included in the TLV Length field, though they are included in the LLS Data Length field in the block header. Unrecognized TLV types are ignored.

One TLV is defined by this document for announcing capabilities and signalling. The Extended Options and Flags TLV has a Type value of 1 and a Value field of 4 bytes, and it must only appear once in the block. Bits in its value have no meaning to the link-local signaling mechanism itself, but bits may be allocated to announce OSPF link-local capabilities, and bits may also be allocated to perform boolean link-local signaling. Two such bits are assigned: the LSDB Resynchronization bit at 0x00000001 and the Restart Signal bit at 0x00000002.

LLS type values in the range of 32768 to 65535 are reserved for private use, and the first four octets of the Value field must be the private enterprise code, which allows multiple vendor extensions to coexist in a network. The criteria for allocating LLS TLVs are that LLS should not be used for information that would be better suited to a link-local link state advertisement, that LLS should be confined to signaling between direct neighbours, and that discretion should be used in the volume of information signalled because of the obvious MTU and performance implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the block is a list of small numbered records. Each one says what it is, how long it is, and holds the data. A router that meets a record it does not know skips it and carries on.

sections.title: Authenticating the Block
sections.content:
A special TLV is used for cryptographic authentication of the LLS data block in OSPFv2. This TLV must only be included in the LLS block when cryptographic authentication is enabled on the corresponding interface. The message digest of the LLS block must be calculated using the same key and authentication algorithm as used for the OSPFv2 packet. The cryptographic sequence number is included in the TLV and must be the same as the one in the OSPFv2 authentication data for the LLS block to be considered authentic.

The TLV holds a Type value of 2, a Length field covering the four bytes of the sequence number and the length of the message digest block, the sequence number itself, and the authentication data. The sequence number is the cryptographic sequence number used to prevent simple replay attacks, and for the LLS block to be considered authentic it must match the sequence number in the OSPFv2 packet header authentication field, which must be present. In the event of a sequence number mismatch or an authentication failure, the whole LLS block must be ignored.

The TLV must not appear more than once in the block, and when present it must be the last TLV in the block. If it appears more than once, only the first occurrence is processed and any others must be ignored. The authentication data contains the message digest calculated for the LLS data block up to the authentication data field itself, which therefore excludes it.

The TLV is not applicable to OSPFv3 and must not be added to any OSPFv3 packet; if found on reception it must be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: When the link already uses cryptographic authentication, the extra block is signed with the same key, so a neighbour that receives it can be sure nobody tampered with it. The signing record goes last in the block and carries a counter that must match the one in the packet header.

sections.title: Compatibility with Routers That Do Not Know LLS
sections.content:
The modifications to the OSPF packet formats are compatible with standard OSPF, because routers that do not support LLS will ignore the LLS data block after the OSPF packet or the cryptographic message digest. As of the writing of this document there were implementations deployed with software compliant to the experimental specification; routers not implementing it ignore the LLS data at the end of the OSPF packet.

Careful consideration should be given to carrying additional LLS data, as it may affect the OSPF adjacency bring-up time due to additional propagation delay and processing time.
sections.plainLanguage: An old router reads the packet, stops at the end of what it understands, and ignores the rest. The cost is a little more work and a slightly slower handshake when the block carries a lot of data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations inherited from OSPFv2 are described in the OSPFv2 specification. The technique provides the same level of security as the basic OSPFv2 protocol by allowing LLS data to be authenticated using the same cryptographic authentication that OSPFv2 uses.

Security considerations inherited from OSPFv3 are described in the OSPFv3 and OSPFv3 authentication documents. OSPFv3 uses IPsec for authentication and encryption. With IPsec, the Authentication Header, the Encapsulating Security Payload, or both are applied to the entire OSPFv3 payload including the LLS block.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra data gets the same protection as the rest of the protocol. In OSPFv2 that means the same signing key; in OSPFv3 the whole packet, extra block included, is covered by IPsec.

items.title: Type
items.text: The identifier of the triplet, unique for each type.

items.text: The length of the Value field, in bytes.

items.title: 32-bit alignment
items.text: All triplets must be 32-bit aligned, with padding if necessary.

items.text: Padding bytes are not included in the Length field, though they are included in the LLS Data Length field.

items.title: Unknown types are ignored
items.text: Unrecognized triplet types are ignored by the receiver.

items.desc: A 4-byte value carrying link-local capability and signal bits. Must appear only once.

viz.caption: The bits assigned inside the Extended Options and Flags triplet
The rules for signing the block

items.title: Same key and algorithm
items.text: The message digest of the LLS block must be calculated using the same key and authentication algorithm as the OSPFv2 packet.

items.title: The sequence number must match
items.text: The cryptographic sequence number in the triplet must be the same as the one in the OSPFv2 packet header authentication field, or the block is not authentic.

items.title: Mismatch discards the block
items.text: On a sequence number mismatch or an authentication failure, the whole LLS block must be ignored.

items.title: Last in the block
items.text: The authentication triplet must not appear more than once, and when present it must be the last one in the block.

items.title: Not for OSPFv3
items.text: It is not applicable to OSPFv3 and must not be added to any OSPFv3 packet; if found on reception it must be ignored.

viz.caption: What happens when the neighbour is old

items.title: Old routers skip it
items.text: Routers that do not support LLS ignore the data block after the OSPF packet or the cryptographic message digest.

items.title: The earlier experiment
items.text: Implementations of the experimental specification were already deployed, and routers without it ignore the LLS data at the end of the packet.

items.title: Routing is unaffected
items.text: Changes made because of the block do not affect basic routing when interacting with routers that do not understand LLS.

items.title: It is not free
items.text: Carrying extra LLS data may slow adjacency bring-up because of additional propagation delay and processing time.
